The emergency guideline for implementing and managing contact tracing for Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) was developed by WHO in collaboration with the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the High-Risk Unaffected Countries Team of the International Task Force for the 2014 Ebola Response. The document is based on guidance from the WHO African Region’s Disease Surveillance and Response Programme. It acknowledges contributions from numerous experts and organizations. The purpose of the document is to address the scale, duration, and complexity of the EVD outbreak in West Africa, emphasizing the need for prompt and effective containment measures. EVD is transmissible as soon as symptoms appear, making it critical to identify and isolate symptomatic individuals immediately. Contact tracing is a vital tool to break transmission chains and control outbreaks. It involves identifying, assessing, and managing individuals exposed to the disease to prevent further spread. Exposed individuals are monitored for 21 days, the maximum incubation period, to quickly identify and isolate symptomatic cases, reducing exposure to others and improving survival rates through timely treatment. Contact tracing has proven effective in halting EVD transmission during past outbreaks. However, the 2014 West Africa outbreak presented challenges, including the outbreak’s geographic spread, resource limitations, community resistance, and restricted access to affected areas. The lack of standardized procedures for contact tracing led to delays and inefficiencies, contributing to ongoing transmission. This operational document provides guidance for implementing and managing contact tracing in countries preparing for or managing EVD outbreaks. It also addresses common challenges and offers solutions, emphasizing monitoring and evaluation of the process. The guide is intended for countries preparing to implement contact tracing and those already engaged in such activities. It is designed for use by national and sub-national emergency management committees, epidemiologists, surveillance officers, and volunteer organizations involved in EVD preparedness and response. The guide should be adapted to local contexts. Contact tracing is a critical component of EVD outbreak control but is only one aspect of a multifaceted strategy. It is closely linked to case finding (surveillance) and case investigation. Detecting an EVD case triggers the investigation process, during which contacts are identified, initiating contact tracing. These efforts depend on other response components, such as social mobilization, logistics, case management, and laboratory capacity. Effective contact tracing requires immediate implementation after case detection and efficient management, necessitating a comprehensive response strategy. Community participation and cooperation are essential for effective contact tracing. Building trust between public health officials and the community is crucial. Engaging local leaders, stakeholders, and volunteers early in response planning fosters community ownership and trust in the health system. Communities must feel confident in cooperating with case investigation and contact tracing teams and supporting the referral of symptomatic contacts to isolation and treatment facilities. Effective communication and culturally sensitive messaging are vital to avoid counterproductive practices and stigma. Public misinterpretations of contact lists as lists of individuals likely to die can lead to resistance and hinder contact tracing efforts. Health communication, messaging, and psychosocial support are critical to overcoming these challenges. Successful contact tracing requires skills in assessing EVD symptoms, interviewing, and counseling. Contact tracers must have investigative skills to identify and track all potential contacts and analyze evidence. They must also be empathetic and flexible to build trust with cases, contacts, and their families. Insufficient expertise and disregard for individual, community, social, cultural, and religious sensitivities can alienate communities and undermine contact tracing efforts. However, contact tracing activities can also establish strong community partnerships. The implementation of contact tracing varies depending on the disease burden and local context. The number of EVD cases and contacts traced daily may cover large geographic areas, including densely populated urban regions, posing logistical challenges. Comprehensive and systematic contact tracing must be supported by robust community engagement and intensified social mobilization. Active case finding should be conducted alongside contact tracing to detect other symptomatic individuals in defined areas. Effective contact tracing requires strict adherence to definitions of “contact” and “EVD case” to promptly identify all contacts and cases. Failure to apply correct definitions can result in ongoing transmission. Developing a local definition of an EVD “alert” with less stringent criteria than an EVD case can help detect infected individuals earlier. All alerts should be investigated to determine if they meet the EVD case definition. Planning and preparation are essential for effective contact tracing. This includes identifying and allocating the necessary infrastructure, personnel, resources, and funding before the first EVD case is detected. An incident management framework should be established, with organized teams led by an incident manager authorized to make immediate decisions, allocate resources, and coordinate ministries. An alert system should operate at national and sub-national levels, with a toll-free hotline for event-based surveillance. Staff involved in the alert system must understand alert and case definitions, EVD signs and symptoms, and how to activate the system. Once activated, the alert system should deploy trained staff to assess suspected cases, ensure safe specimen collection, and transport cases to treatment facilities if needed.
